question: How does whale oil become an industry, and how do the Reformation and the Atlantic reshuffle the fats of Europe and the world?
thesis: Between 1500 and 1750 fat becomes a matter of states and oceans. Whaling turns into a chartered, armed and taxed industry; the Atlantic moves pigs, olive oil, palm oil and sesame between continents, some of it in the holds of slave ships; and the Reformation turns the old split between butter and oil into a quarrel over religion and health. Asia has its own story of ranked oils, lamps, frying and ghee.

big_ideas.title: Whale oil becomes an industry of states
big_ideas.text: The Basques open a station at Red Bay, Elizabeth grants a monopoly, English and Dutch ships fight over Spitsbergen, and the Navigation Act of 1651 and the duties of 1672 protect English whale oil. A warm decade drives the whales offshore, and soap-boilers in Leith put money into a voyage.

big_ideas.title: The Atlantic carries fats between continents
big_ideas.text: Columbus’s eight pigs, Spanish olive oil and then olive trees go west; palm oil goes from Angola and São Tomé to Brazil and seasons the gruel on slave ships; sesame travels as the African benne. The sunflower and the coconut reach Europe.

big_ideas.title: Butter against oil becomes a quarrel of religion and health
big_ideas.text: Luther rails at the Lenten oil and the sale of butter dispensations, a cardinal travels with his own olive oil to avoid the butter that supposedly breeds lepers, Carnival fights Lent in street drama, and butter becomes a status symbol in Italy and the pride of the Dutch ‘butterboxes’.

big_ideas.title: Light, soap and tallow show the limits of supply
big_ideas.text: London fines soap-makers who use anything but pure olive oil; its tallow chandlers cannot make enough candles; and 24,000 lights burn in the park at Versailles as a show of wealth.

big_ideas.title: Asia ranks, presses and fries its oils
big_ideas.text: Song Yingxing ranks the oils of Ming China and describes the wedge press, and the peanut arrives from America; Edo Japan lights its homes with vegetable oil, learns tempura and organises net whaling; Java fries in oil; Vijayanagara’s king drinks sesame oil and Bengal ships its butter.

threads.title: Whaling as a state industry
threads.claim: From Basque stations to Anglo-Dutch war, whale oil is a matter for charters, navies and customs.

beats.text: The Basques run a whaling station at Red Bay, Labrador, the first found in North America.
Elizabeth I gives the Muscovy Company a twenty-year monopoly to hunt whales in any seas.
Basque harpooners lead the English to Spitsbergen, and the Dutch build a whale-oil industry there.
English and Dutch whalers fight over Spitsbergen, the English arming their ships.
A warm decade moves the whales offshore and makes shore whaling harder.
Massachusetts and Southampton regulate drift whales cast ashore.
The Navigation Act and the 1672 duties favour English whale oil over Dutch.
Van Riebeeck sees thousands of whales in Table Bay but has nowhere to store the oil.
Soap-boilers of Leith invest £1,700 in a whaling voyage that returns £525 profit.

threads.title: Plants, pigs and oils cross the oceans
threads.claim: The Atlantic world swaps fats: Old World animals and oils west, African palm oil and sesame across, and New World plants east.

beats.text: The coconut is described by a friar about 1292 and becomes known in Europe after the Portuguese reach the Indian Ocean.
Columbus’s eight pigs of 1493 become herds from Hispaniola to Virginia, and their fatty flesh becomes salt pork.
American demand stimulates Spanish olive oil, then religious orders plant olives across South America.
The sunflower, from eastern North America, is illustrated in Dodoens’s herbal.
John Barbot reports Guinea’s people seasoning food, lighting lamps and anointing themselves with palm oil.
Women captives on slave ships pound and boil palm fruits for the oil in the gruel.
A Dutch ledger records palm oil and kernels moving from Angola and São Tomé to Brazil.
Britain hopes colonial sesame will replace imported olive oil, and Africans bring benne to the American South.

threads.title: Butter against oil after Luther
threads.claim: The old geography of butter and oil becomes a fight over faith and health.

beats.text: Carnival, with butter at the head of the animal fats, wars on Lent and its olive oil in paintings and street drama.
Once the north gets butter in Lent, Italy follows and butter becomes a status symbol.
The Cardinal of Aragon travels through Flanders with his own oil, since butter countries are said to be overrun with lepers.
Luther says Rome forces northerners to eat an oil they would not use on their shoes, then sells the right to eat butter.
Holland becomes the foremost dairy power, its ‘butterboxes’ fed by grazing soil built from manure and soap-ash.

threads.title: Soap, candles and the limits of supply
threads.claim: Fat as light and soap is scarce and policed.

beats.text: London fines and jails soap-makers who use any oil but pure olive oil.
About 24,000 lights burn at Versailles, a display of wealth in wax.
Houghton finds London’s five million pounds of tallow a year is not enough for the chandlers.

threads.title: China: the peanut, the ranking and the press
threads.claim: A Ming scholar sets out which oil is for eating and which for burning, and a new American crop arrives.

beats.text: The peanut crosses from America to China by way of the Portuguese, and is grown for export by 1700.
Song Yingxing ranks oils by use: sesame best for eating, tallow-tree kernel for lamps.
The Tiangong kaiwu describes the wedge press: roast, roll, steam and press twice.

threads.title: Lamps, frying and ghee in Southeast Asia, Japan and India
threads.claim: Evening light and frying fats are the two uses that stand out in the Asian travellers’ and household records.

beats.text: Southeast Asia lights its evenings with kemiri-nut oil and damar rather than wax.
The king of Vijayanagara drinks three-quarters of a pint of sesame oil before dawn and anoints himself with it.
Tempura arrives in Japan from Portuguese cooking.
In Edo Japan vegetable-oil lamps and candles enter ordinary homes.
Taiji’s whalers organise in five crews in 1606 and use nets by about 1677.
A Dutch observer says Java feasts fry in oil where the Dutch use butter.
John Fryer finds Bengal’s butter, probably ghee, shipped by sea to ‘numberless places’.

turning_points.text: Columbus brings the first pigs to the New World.
Luther attacks the Lenten oil and the butter dispensations.
The Basques found a whaling station at Red Bay.
Elizabeth I grants a whaling monopoly.
English and Dutch whalers fight over Spitsbergen.
London polices what soap-makers put in their kettles.
Song Yingxing ranks the oils of China.
Palm oil crosses from Angola to Brazil.
England’s Navigation Act protects its whale oil.
Twenty-four thousand lights burn at Versailles.
London’s tallow chandlers cannot meet demand.

text: Fifteen entries: whaling as a state industry at Spitsbergen, Elizabeth’s monopoly and the Navigation Act, soap fines, the Lenten oil fight from Luther to the Dutch ‘butterboxes’, tallow chandlers and the lights of Versailles ([[c1]], [[o1]], [[o3]], [[o2]], [[b1]], [[e1]], [[ec5]], [[ec8]], [[e2]]).
No entry. The Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal worlds are missing; the Cairo Geniza of the folio before ends in the Middle Ages and no early-modern source for the region is held.

Ming China ranks the oils and describes the wedge press; the coconut becomes known in Europe from the Indian Ocean; Vijayanagara’s king drinks sesame oil and Bengal ships its butter ([[ec15]], [[ec16]]); Southeast Asia fries in oil and lights its evenings with kemiri-nut oil and damar; the peanut arrives in China from America; and Edo Japan organises its net whalers, grows rapeseed for lamps and takes tempura from the Portuguese ([[th3]], [[te1]], [[ec9]], [[ec12]], [[ec13]], [[x2]], [[ec17]], [[ec14]], [[e3]]).

Four entries, three about Africa as a source for others: palm oil crossing to Brazil, on the slave ship’s pot, and the Guinea coast’s own uses ([[ec4]], [[l1]], [[ec10]]); and the Cape’s unworked whales ([[ec11]]). The African voices are Barbot’s and Van Riebeeck’s, both European.

Five entries: Red Bay and the colonial whale laws, sesame and *benne* in the American South, olive oil to Spanish America, and the pigs that cross the Atlantic from Columbus’s eight in 1493 to Jamestown’s hundreds, whose fatty flesh becomes salt pork ([[ec1]], [[o4]], [[ec6]], [[x1]], [[ec18]]).

sources.intro: Ellis's whaling history and Dolin's American whaling carry the industry; Khosrova, Flandrin and Mueller the butter and oil politics; Zuckerman and Lynn the palm oil; Needham the Chinese side.
main: Khosrova, Flandrin and Mueller ([[b1]], [[th1]], [[e1]], [[ec5]], [[ec7]], [[o2]]); Kiple for the sunflower, coconut and sesame ([[th2]], [[ec9]], [[ec6]]).
Zuckerman and Lynn for palm oil ([[ec4]], [[l1]]); Needham for China ([[th3]], [[te1]]); Lowengard for tallow ([[ec8]]); Schivelbusch for Versailles ([[e2]]).
Lynn for Barbot’s palm oil ([[ec10]]); Ellis for Table Bay ([[ec11]]).
Reid for Southeast Asia ([[ec12]], [[ec13]]); Ishige for Japan ([[ec14]], [[e3]]).
Bray and Anderson for the peanut in China ([[x2]]).
Achaya for Vijayanagara and Bengal ([[ec15]], [[ec16]]); Ellis for Japanese whaling ([[ec17]]).
Kiple (Gade) for the pigs of the Americas ([[ec18]]).
contested: Flandrin's idea that oil-hatred helped drive the Reformation ([[b1]]).
The 1618 soap-oil fines are reported without the order ([[o2]]).
Palm oil on the slave ship rests on a popular history with period examples ([[l1]]).
gaps: No source for Mexican and Peruvian oil production under Spanish rule; none for Indian fats in the Mughal period.
Dutch and Danish primary records of whaling and the Hamburg trade were not read.

The Ottoman and Safavid worlds, Oceania and most of Africa have no entry in these centuries; Barbot and Van Riebeeck are European observers of African fats, and India appears only through foreign travellers’ eyes.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.
The whale entries are the longest connected chain; follow them through *Economy*, *Order* and *Conflict*. *Belief* and *Thought* carry the Reformation fat line.
The Nexus shows how the whaling rivalry and the soap trade connect.
The *picture by region* counts the 35 entries: Europe 15, Far East 11, Africa 4, Americas 5; none in Near East, Oceania or Worldwide. Europe dominates, and the Near East has no entry.
